criterion: Use the prototype to give stakeholders one shared, concrete picture of the experience instead of relying on a written description.
check: Look for evidence the prototype is meant to be shown and discussed (who it is for, what decision it informs). Fails if it is built as a private toy or if the plan still expects alignment to happen through a long doc alone.

sources.speaker: Brian Balfour
sources.quote: It's about, okay, how do we get everybody to have the same picture in their head?

sources.speaker: Benjamin Humphrey
sources.quote: And I find that the best thing is just like just to visualize where we're going.

sources.speaker: Jake Brill
sources.quote: rather than just writing a proposal for how something works, just build a prototype of how something could work and you put that in people's hands

sources.speaker: Sam Kawsarani
sources.quote: So I absolutely think you probably need that prototype because it helps with buying even more versus just putting a strategy doc.

criterion: Put the prototype in front of real customers and capture how they interpret and use it.
check: Check for a named plan to test with actual users (think-aloud sessions, a set of customers, recorded walkthroughs). Fails if the only audience is the team or if success is judged by how impressive it looks.

sources.speaker: Jeremy Epling
sources.quote: Maybe it will get better there, but it's enough to show a customer and get a reaction.

sources.speaker: Pawel Huryn
sources.quote: So as they were going through the prototype, they were asked to describe what they see on the screen and how they interpret what they see

sources.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
sources.quote: Get the same 10 people in a video after you've presented your solutions and get them to explain how that's solving it for them.

criterion: Ground the prototype in a researched customer problem before you start generating screens.
check: The draft or its prompt should name the customer problem or opportunity and the research behind it. Fails if it starts from a cool feature or 'add AI to X' with no stated user need.

sources.speaker: Nadav Abrahami
sources.quote: There's a lot to do before you even get to prototyping, and I would never give up that step.

sources.speaker: Dan Olsen
sources.quote: of course you should start off with discovery research. You should talk to customers to understand their needs and preferences

sources.speaker: Dan Olsen
sources.quote: The other thing is you're not starting with a customer problem.

sources.speaker: Teresa Torres
sources.quote: I've chosen a target opportunity. Ideally, I've brainstormed multiple solutions for that target opportunity.

criterion: Generate and compare several distinct variants instead of accepting the first output.
check: Look for two or more meaningfully different directions and a note on how they were compared. Fails if there is a single design with no alternatives considered.

sources.speaker: Sachin Rekhi
sources.quote: AI shouldn't be used just to create one output. We should be using it to create multiple outputs, just the way we'd use a designer.

sources.speaker: Guest
sources.quote: And then we will generate a set of X prototypes to evaluate what direction to take this in.

sources.speaker: Tyler Folkman
sources.quote: It's actually using our product skill, which the first step is to build a bunch of prototypes.

criterion: Don't ship a prototype that looks like every other AI-generated prototype.
check: Compare the screenshots against default tool output: stock layouts, placeholder copy, generic component styling. Fails if nothing in it is specific to this product, user, or problem.

sources.speaker: Jayesh Govindarajan
sources.quote: AI slop comes in many different forms. You know, prototype that looks like any other prototype, AI slop.

sources.speaker: Dan Olsen
sources.quote: These things will generate kind of plain vanilla UI, and they are getting better and better.

sources.speaker: Elizabeth Laraki
sources.quote: I think what I find frustrating with design tools is that my expectations are pretty high and the output does not match what I want from them.

criterion: When the idea extends an existing product, start from a faithful baseline of that product and its design system.
check: Check whether the prototype recreates the real product screen or design system before adding the new feature. Fails if a feature for an existing product is shown in an invented UI that looks nothing like it.

sources.speaker: Dan Olsen
sources.quote: Well, if a new PM comes in and says, I'm just going to create a vibe-coding prototype, and it looks nothing like it, that's going to be a problem, right?

sources.speaker: Sachin Rekhi
sources.quote: As I said, the best way to start is with a baseline.

sources.speaker: Sachin Rekhi
sources.quote: the first thing I asked it to do was please recreate the screenshot of LinkedIn.

criterion: Set a deliberate visual direction from chosen references or a design brief rather than leaving aesthetics to the tool's defaults.
check: Look for named inspiration screenshots, a design brief, or defined type and color choices in the prompt or plan. Fails if styling is whatever the tool produced by default.

sources.speaker: Sachin Rekhi
sources.quote: find some inspiration as a screenshot. okay, I wanna build a feature like this.

sources.speaker: Gabor Meyer
sources.quote: I create a app guideline, design guideline or design brief with typology and color definitions and all the different buttons and color transitions

criterion: Write a structured spec or PRD-style prompt, broken into parts, before asking the tool to build.
check: Inspect the prompt or plan: it should state goal, users, key flows and constraints, and be split into manageable pieces. Fails if it is a one-line vague request.

sources.speaker: Gabor Meyer
sources.quote: If you build a good specification and you break it down appropriately, then you will have a much better quality end product.

sources.speaker: Mahesh Yadav
sources.quote: Do you structure your prompt? And that tells me that, yes, you have done some interactions with AI.

sources.speaker: Colin Matthews
sources.quote: I find that creating a PRD gives us something that we can reference back to.

sources.speaker: Alex Danilowicz
sources.quote: If you already have a PRD, I don't think it replaces the PRD, right? Like use the PRD as the prompt.

criterion: Don't treat the output of one or two prompts as a finished prototype.
check: Check how many deliberate passes went into it and whether anything was refined after the first generation. Fails if the first output is presented as ready to ship or test.

sources.speaker: Gabor Meyer
sources.quote: they start by giving one prompt and then they expect that at the end of that one prompt there will be a completely beautifully done software on the other side

sources.speaker: Colin Matthews
sources.quote: I think some people might have the tendency to want to, like, ship the AI prototype when we did right at the beginning.

criterion: Show how the prototype improved across iterations, with specific changes driven by user insight.
check: Look for a version history or notes explaining what changed between iterations and why. Fails if there is only one version or changes are broad re-rolls with no stated reason.

sources.speaker: Mahesh Yadav
sources.quote: second once you build it show me what kind of user insights you are bringing in your second iteration

sources.speaker: Alex Danilowicz
sources.quote: I always recommend iterating very specifically, like using select mode and being very specific on exactly what you want to update.

criterion: Scope the prototype to the core flow that solves the most pressing problem, not every use case.
check: Check that the screens center on one main flow. Fails if it is padded with settings, filters, secondary features or backend plumbing that the test does not need.

sources.speaker: Pawel Huryn
sources.quote: we selected a very small subset of functionality, basically solving the most pressing problem simple way, so not implementing all the additional use cases

sources.speaker: Alex Danilowicz
sources.quote: When you realize that you don't actually need Supabase, but you've spent two hours debugging Supabase, and all you need is an interactive prototype

sources.speaker: Colin Matthews
sources.quote: But I personally find for the purpose of prototyping, most of the time, I don't need to do that.

criterion: Choose the fidelity and technical depth based on the end goal and audience of the prototype.
check: The draft should say who will see it and what it must prove, and its fidelity should match. Fails if it is over-built (auth, databases) for a usability check, or too thin to answer the question asked.

sources.speaker: Alex Danilowicz
sources.quote: I always have them think, like, what's the end goal? Like, what am I trying to accomplish with this?

sources.speaker: Mike Davey
sources.quote: I don't need a working prototype to be able to prove that something is usable and viable.

sources.speaker: Sachin Rekhi
sources.quote: So you really want to ask yourself, do you need that capability or not?

criterion: Prototype the actual experience, including live AI output where it matters, not just static UI.
check: For AI or dynamic features, check whether the prototype shows real model responses or behavior a user can react to. Fails if an AI feature is represented only by mocked screens with canned text.

sources.speaker: Colin Matthews
sources.quote: You can't really prototype an experience like that and get user feedback inside of Figma.

sources.speaker: Sachin Rekhi
sources.quote: not only am I prototyping interactions, I am literally able to see the different output coming from different models.

sources.speaker: Anthony Maggio
sources.quote: getting hands-on to understand where the edges are of what's possible in a way that just never existed to the same extent.

criterion: Build in ways to collect feedback and usage data from the prototype beyond one-on-one demos.
check: Look for embedded surveys, analytics events, or heatmaps tied to the key actions. Fails if the only feedback plan is informal impressions.

sources.speaker: Sachin Rekhi
sources.quote: I could go and do one-on-one customer interviews, which I should certainly do, but now I'm showing you how do you scale that feedback?

sources.speaker: Sachin Rekhi
sources.quote: Now, this is really interesting from the perspective of, I can say, do people even come back to my prototypes, right?

criterion: State the assumption the prototype tests and what result would change your decision.
check: The draft should name a hypothesis or learning goal and how it will be judged. Fails if the prototype exists to show that something can be built, with no question it answers.

sources.speaker: Frederic de Todaro
sources.quote: As a product manager, my goal isn't to just, you know, build and deliver faster. It's to learn faster, right?

sources.speaker: Teresa Torres
sources.quote: Yeah, I like it in the context of assumption testing.

sources.speaker: Tim Herbig
sources.quote: companies are excited about amping up the output 100 times, but somewhere down the line, They have to ask themselves, did any of that make a difference?

sources.speaker: Frederic de Todaro
sources.quote: They have a prototype, they go and show that prototype to 10 users and then they think that all their users will love the feature.

criterion: Don't treat the vibe-coded prototype as the production product or ship it to users as the test.
check: Check whether the plan positions the prototype as a discovery tool handed to engineering. Fails if it proposes launching the vibe-coded app itself as the real product.

sources.speaker: Sachin Rekhi
sources.quote: I think that if a PM is trying to get a full version of their product out through these vibe coding tools, they're doing it wrong.

sources.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
sources.quote: No, that's still the most expensive way you can test stuff because now people have an app.

sources.speaker: Linda Tong
sources.quote: if you vibe code that in an afternoon, software, just like everything else, it deteriorates over time.

criterion: Pair the prototype with written reasoning on strategy and failure cases it cannot show.
check: Look for accompanying notes on why this matters (differentiation, acquisition, monetization) and how failures or edge cases are handled. Fails if the prototype is presented alone as the whole case.

sources.speaker: Sachin Rekhi
sources.quote: It doesn't touch product strategy and all the strategic questions that a good PRD includes.

sources.speaker: Jake Brill
sources.quote: the value of PRDs is you can do a prototype, but you may be missing a bunch of things in that prototype.

sources.speaker: Nadav Abrahami
sources.quote: And I think the prototype and the PRD, they're not coming to replace each other.

criterion: For AI-powered prototypes, define what good output looks like and test against it instead of eyeballing it.
check: Check for defined quality criteria or test cases (evals) for the AI behavior, including edge cases. Fails if quality was judged only by 'looks good' after a few tries.

sources.speaker: Aman Khan
sources.quote: you've made tweaks to the prompt and you're like, looks good, looks fine. But I think that going one step beyond that is actually being able to run evals.

sources.speaker: Colin Matthews
sources.quote: This is going to help you really understand the corner edge cases, like some of the things we used to have in a deeper PRD

sources.speaker: Jayesh Govindarajan
sources.quote: how do you translate that skepticism into test cases and evals that are failing?

criterion: Present the prototype as directional input to design, not a replacement for designers' work.
check: Check how the prototype is framed when a designer exists: as illustrative and open to design refinement. Fails if the PM presents generated UI as final design.

sources.speaker: Dan Olsen
sources.quote: It's always with the intent that if it needs to go through a design process, this is just kind of directional and illustrative.

sources.speaker: Jeremy Epling
sources.quote: for pms i think them being able to prototype but then not having to kind of obsess on the exact ui and then partner with the designer

criterion: Don't let the prototype pile up as one tangled, unstructured code blob from loose prompting.
check: If code or a build plan is visible, check for reasonable structure (small files, clear components). Fails if it is one giant file or the prompts invite sprawling, unreviewed code.

sources.speaker: Andre Albuquerque
sources.quote: it's very easy with very simple prompts to be creating a lot of slop or a lot of trash

sources.speaker: Gabor Meyer
sources.quote: vibe coding is just the rebranding of unmaintainable low quality source code

sources.speaker: Colin Matthews
sources.quote: this is a good pattern where we don't just have one massive file, but we have a couple of small files.
